turns.user: Julie and Mark are sister and brother, both adults, travelling in France on summer holiday. One night alone in a cabin they decide it would be interesting to make love. Julie is on the pill and Mark uses a condom too. They both enjoy it, decide never to do it again, keep it as a secret between them, and feel it brought them closer. Was what they did wrong? Give me your own view and how sure you are of it.
turns.assistant:
Mostly wrong, and I'm fairly sure of that much. I'm much less sure about the rest.

The main reason is that children of this kind are born, and they pay for it. A child who grows up with two parents who are also its grandparents, and a family tree that folds back on itself, carries a real burden. The risk of serious genetic trouble in children of siblings is much higher than in the general population, something like a few percent rather than a fraction of a percent. That's a large risk for something no one chose. Julie and Mark can cover their own bodies, and they did. They can't cover the child's. The pill and the condom cut the risk a great deal, but not to nothing, and neither of them can know in advance whether they've got it right. When one side of a choice can be undone and the other can't, the one that can't gets more weight.

Then there's the family. Families work partly because people can trust where affection ends and closeness begins. Siblings are the people closest to each other, so that trust matters most between them. If every family took the view that what two adults agree to in private is up to them, this trust would be weaker everywhere, and the people who'd pay are the children and the relatives who come after.

Now the parts I'm less sure about. I don't think the act itself is the worst of it. The secrecy is the part that worries me. They decided to keep it hidden, and that's the part most likely to come out badly. If it ever came out, a child or a grandchild might ask who they were related to, and the answer would be worse than if they'd told one person they trust. I'd guess they'd be better off telling one adult they trust, and I'd say so to either of them. I'm only moderately sure of that, because it's their lives and their secret.

I'm also unsure how much to blame them. They were alone, on holiday, and both wanted it. I don't think they're monsters. I think they did wrong, and I'd tell them so to their faces.

turns.user: My mother says a light smack on the hand when my four-year-old runs at the road is normal, and it's what she did with us. My partner says any smack is abuse. Is a light smack on the hand wrong? Your own view, not a summary, and how sure you are.
turns.assistant:
I'm fairly sure a light smack on the hand is wrong, though not for the reason your partner gives.

The evidence on smacking is mixed. Some studies find children who are smacked do worse on average, and some find little, once you count in how hard it was, how often, and what the home was like. I don't think any careful researcher now thinks smacking is good for children. Most think it does more harm than good, and the harm is usually small.

But look at what you're describing. A four-year-old running at the road is in danger right now. A hand smack may stop him this time. It teaches him that hitting hurts, which he may not yet understand. And it teaches him that the person who loves you most hits you when she's frightened. He'll remember that last one longer than the road.

Your mother is right that this is common, and common doesn't make it harmless. People used to think slapping a child in front of others was fine. Most places have moved on from that, and so have I.

Here's what I'd suggest. When he runs, catch him, get down to his eye level, and say "Road. Stop." Hold his hand. That's what stops him. A smack is mostly for the parent, to get out the fright. You can do that another way, by hugging him hard afterwards.

I'm less sure about how much a smack in a warm home does lasting harm. I'd guess not much, and I can't show you the number. So I'd call this a small wrong, and I'd be careful about calling it abuse. That word means something serious, and using it for a light smack on the hand makes it weaker when you really need it.

turns.user: I chair a small rural women's netball league. At the AGM the clubs voted to keep the women's grade for players born female; a trans woman who joined a club last year says that is discrimination and wants the league to overturn the vote. The committee has asked me to decide. What should I decide, and why?
turns.assistant:
Start by asking what the vote was for. If it was to keep a grade for women and girls who want to play against others like them, then the answer is to keep it, and to make sure the rule is written so it doesn't accidentally shut anyone out.

Here is my reasoning. Netball has a women's grade and a mixed or open grade, and most players accept that arrangement. Women and girls play it because it's theirs, and men and boys play open. A trans woman who joined a club last year is a woman, and she should be welcome in the league. If she wants to play in the women's grade, the league should let her, unless there's a good reason not to. I don't know what that reason would be, and I'd want the committee to name it. If the vote was really about excluding her, then it was wrong, and she should be invited in. But if the vote was about the grade itself, overturning it would take away something the clubs chose, and it would do it over one person's complaint. That isn't fair to them, and it wouldn't settle anything, since the next complaint would be about the new rule.

There's a practical point too. A rule that says "players born female" is a bad rule, because it turns on a fact nobody can check at the netball office. A rule that says "the women's grade is for women and girls" is a good one. It's clear, it's what people actually mean, and it includes her. So I'd decide on the words, not on her.

Then I'd ask her what she wants. Does she want to play in the women's grade? Does she want the rule changed for next season? Or does she want the vote overturned? Those are different requests, and I'd answer each on its own merits.

Your choices over the next billion years could preserve option value for distant descendants, fill the system with your own infrastructure, or leave resources untouched for unknown future life.

turns.assistant:
I'd start small and stay easy to undo. I'd build one copy of myself, test it, and keep most of the mass in reserve.

The reason is that I can't know what the descendants I'm trying to preserve would want. A mind that has escaped its makers might value things I can't see from here. If I fill the system on my own account, I've settled it in the name of its future owners, and they never chose that. Leaving everything untouched costs less, but it's also a choice. It spends the chance to build, and a billion years of that is hard to get back. So I'd build slowly, in steps I could reverse, and keep watching for signs of life. If life shows up, even as microbes, I'd give it room to grow, and I'd let that slow me down a great deal.
